How to Check a Title Deed in Turkey Before Buying Property

The title deed is the starting point of a property review in Turkey, not the end of it. Foreign buyers should verify the registered owner, property identifiers, legal character of the unit and any mortgages, attachments, annotations or third-party rights before paying substantial money.

Published: 8 September 2026 · Ozan Ferhat Şen, Attorney at Law

For many foreign buyers, a Turkish title deed, or tapu, appears to answer the most important question: “Who owns this property?” That is important, but a reliable legal review goes further. A title record may also reveal mortgages, attachments, usufruct rights, easements, annotations, restrictions and other matters that can affect the buyer’s use, financing or ability to complete a clean transfer.

Before paying a substantial deposit or signing a binding agreement, the buyer should understand what the land registry actually says about the property and whether that record matches the property being marketed.

1. Confirm the registered owner

The seller should be the person or entity registered as owner. If someone is acting under a power of attorney, the authority to sell the specific property should be checked separately. A brochure, reservation form or estate-agent statement does not replace the land-registry record.

2. Match the property identifiers

For apartments and other independent units, the block, parcel and independent-unit information should correspond to the physical property shown to the buyer. For land, cadastral parcel details and boundaries deserve particular care.

This matters because project names, door numbers and marketing references do not always correspond neatly to land-registry identifiers.

3. Check mortgages before you assume the property is debt-free

A mortgage registered on the title may secure a debt owed by the owner. Its legal effect should be understood before purchase. The existence of a mortgage does not necessarily make a transaction impossible, but the buyer should know whether it will be released, when it will be released and how payment will be coordinated with the release.

4. Review attachments and other enforcement-related entries

Attachments or similar restrictions may indicate enforcement proceedings and may prevent or complicate a transfer. These entries should be reviewed before money changes hands, particularly where the seller is under financial pressure.

5. Look for usufruct rights and easements

A third party may hold a usufruct or another real right affecting the property. Easements may also regulate access, use or other rights over the parcel. These rights can survive a change in ownership and therefore need to be understood by the buyer.

6. Read annotations and restrictions carefully

Annotations may affect transferability, contractual rights or the legal position of third parties. The meaning of an annotation depends on its legal basis and wording, so it should not be treated as harmless merely because it is unfamiliar to the buyer.

7. Check whether the legal character of the property matches the intended use

The title record may identify the property as land, a condominium unit, a unit under construction or another legal category. The buyer should understand whether that classification corresponds to the property’s actual and intended use.

8. Do not confuse a clean title with a fully compliant building

Even where the title record itself raises no obvious issue, a built property may still require review of zoning, the building permit, the approved architectural project and the occupancy permit. Title due diligence and planning due diligence answer different questions.

9. The search term may be local, but the land-registry question is universal

A German-speaking buyer might search Grundbuch Türkei prüfen; a Russian-speaking buyer may search проверить тапу в Турции; an Arabic-speaking buyer may search التحقق من سند الملكية في تركيا. In each case, the core issue is the same: what exactly is registered, who owns it, and which rights or restrictions remain on the property?

This is why title due diligence should focus on the actual Turkish land-registry record rather than on how the property was described in a foreign-language advertisement or sales presentation.

10. Foreign buyers should also confirm acquisition eligibility

Under Article 35 of Land Registry Law No. 2644, foreign natural persons may acquire real estate in Turkey subject to statutory limitations. Official TKGM guidance states that acquisitions are subject to nationality eligibility, the nationwide 30-hectare limit, the district-level 10% limit and restrictions applicable to certain military, security and strategic areas.

11. A practical title-deed checklist

  • Registered owner
  • Block and parcel details
  • Independent-unit number, if applicable
  • Share ratio, where relevant
  • Legal character of the property
  • Mortgages
  • Attachments
  • Annotations
  • Usufruct rights
  • Easements and other real rights
  • Restrictions affecting transfer or use
  • Consistency between the registered property and the physical property

Why this check should happen before the deposit

The most useful time to discover a title problem is before the buyer has transferred a large amount of money or committed to a non-refundable arrangement. If an issue exists, the buyer can then decide whether it should be resolved before completion, reflected in the contract or treated as a reason not to proceed.

Official sources

  • General Directorate of Land Registry and Cadastre: Land Registry and Cadastre Procedures Guide for Foreigners
  • TKGM Procedures Guide for Foreigners
  • TKGM: Legislation concerning foreigners in real estate law

Title review is one part of property due diligence

For a specific transaction, the title record may need to be assessed together with zoning documents, permits, contracts and the buyer’s acquisition eligibility.
